newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea strike leaders rebuff court order.
newsitem.headline: South Korea strike leaders rebuff court order.

text.p: Seven militant South Korean strike leaders camped in freezing conditions outside a Seoul cathedral rebuffed police trying to deliver an order for them to appear in court on Friday.
Heads of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions warned any attempt to arrest them would trigger all-out stoppages.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil told a news conference: "If any of the seven, including myself, are arrested, we have orders to start intensive strikes immediately."
Police investigators supported by several hundred riot police burst into confederation headquarters shortly before midnight on Thursday to seize documents.
State prosecutors had requested the court to issue arrest warrants for the seven on charges of obstructing business by staging illegal strikes, but a judge has said he wants to question them first.

A Roman Catholic official urged the government and union leaders to compromise, but said there was nothing clergy could do if police decided to violate sacred ground and storm Myongdong Cathedral property.
"Democracy is the result of talks and cooperation," Chang Bok-pil told reporters. "But there is nothing we can do if the government decides to come in with force."

Meanwhile, international labour union leaders were due to arrive on Saturday to try to persuade the government to scrap a new labour law that has sparked workers' wrath by giving employers the right to lay off staff.
The Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) says the new law is a step backwards towards even greater repression of workers.
The Minister for Labour, Jin Nyum, rejected the allegations, although he conceded the law was not ideal.

"There is nothing in the new law that worsens the rights of workers," he told a news conference. "The law cannot be elevated to that of the OECD overnight," he said, referring to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development that Seoul has newly joined.
"But it is great progress for the better."
The ICFTU filed a complaint with the International Labour Organisation about the law, saying it violated internationally recognised trade union rights.

It complained about provisions allowing strikers to be replaced by outside workers, banning dismissed workers from belonging to unions and prohibiting companies from paying strikers during work stoppages.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung renewed warnings to strikers that they risked punishment, but also appealed for unions and management to work together.
"The government has no alternative but to take stern measures against illegal strikes for the sake of protecting public interests," Lee told businessmen.
"Walkouts resorted to by some workers, who are either unaware of the real intent of the new labour legislation or pursuing political ends, cannot be tolerated."
He said the law would not lower wages or worsen working conditions and was not intended to allow mass layoffs.
Lee called on workers to "stop illegal acts that are causing social unrest at a time when the country is struggling with economic difficulties".
Kwon's outlawed confederation claims that around 200,000 of its 500,000 members are on strike, although the government puts the figure at less than half that number.

On Thursday the largest union body, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions with 1.2 million members, called on workers to join the biggest strike in South Korea's history for two days starting next Tuesday.
